title: Halitosis: Worst Smell Ever?
summary: Josh and Chuck open with a tangent about ASMR-style videos, then turn to halitosis (bad breath). They cover the word's origin in Latin and Greek, how Listerine's 1920s marketing popularized the term and mouthwash, and the bacterial causes of bad breath, including food such as garlic and onions, morning breath, dry mouth (xerostomia), illness, and ketosis. They also cover metabolic breath (liver problems, "mousey" breath), tips for control (brushing, flossing, tongue scraping, water, avoiding antibacterial mouthwash), and how dentists test breath. The episode closes with listener mail about the April Fools' prank in which Ben replaced Chuck, and a birthday shout-out.

segments.title: Opening banter and ASMR tangent
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck joke about listener reviews and discuss ASMR videos, which some people find pleasurable, and agree to research it for a future episode.

segments.title: Halitosis definition and Listerine's marketing history
segments.summary: The hosts introduce halitosis as a clinical term for bad breath. They explain that Listerine, originally a surgical antiseptic, marketed mouthwash in the 1920s by popularizing the medical-sounding word halitosis, which had fallen out of use, to create a self-conscious market. They trace the word to Latin halitus (breath) and Greek -osis (abnormal condition).

segments.title: Personal stories about halitophobia
segments.summary: Josh describes his fear of bad breath, which he calls halitophobia, and a past girlfriend whose breath bothered him. Chuck and Josh talk about being bothered by others' breath in movie theaters and at concerts.

segments.title: Food-related breath: garlic and onions
segments.summary: Garlic and onions are commonly blamed for bad breath. The hosts explain that the compound allicin in garlic converts to allyl methyl sulfide in the stomach, which is absorbed and exhaled through the lungs, so the smell is not just food particles in the mouth. They also discuss garlic pills.

segments.title: Bacteria and the causes of bad breath
segments.summary: The hosts say halitosis comes from bacteria in the mouth, which break down food particles, dead cells, and proteins and release sulfur gases. They note that the average mouth holds many bacterial types, and compare this to armpit odor. Dry mouth overnight causes morning breath, and chronic dry mouth (xerostomia) worsens halitosis. Medications and sinus infections can also contribute.

segments.title: Metabolic breath: liver disease and ketosis
segments.summary: Breath can signal disease. The hosts mention mousey breath from liver failure and fruity breath from ketosis in low-carbohydrate diets, which is caused by ketone bodies released as the body burns fat.

segments.title: Treating bad breath: brushing, tongue scraping, mouthwash, and water
segments.summary: The hosts recommend attacking food particles and bacteria by brushing, flossing, scraping or brushing the tongue, and drinking water. They discuss the British Medical Journal's suggestion of chlorhexidine gluconate mouthwash, and argue against killing all bacteria because a healthy oral ecosystem is beneficial. They suggest brushing after lunch. Breath mints are described as only masking odor.

segments.title: When to see a dentist or doctor, and home remedies
segments.summary: If home care fails, the hosts suggest seeing a dentist or doctor. They describe a dentist's smell test that separates mouth and nasal sources. They also mention home remedies such as a cinnamon and honey rinse and apple cider vinegar, and recommend eating crunchy foods.

segments.title: April Fools' prank listener mail and birthday shout-out
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the April Fools' prank in which Chuck seemingly quit and Ben replaced him, and listener reactions. A listener named Matt from Athens shares that his girlfriend cried, and the hosts give her a birthday shout-out. The sign-off includes social media and contact information.
